en: The Fifth Chapter.
Now, it is asked: what is this novel function called *vyañjanā*?
It is said—Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ka) Since it has been stated that the classification of poetry is based on the classification of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), and since the suggested meaning is apprehended through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*), he asks about this function: "Now, what is this?
He says, "Abhinava" [meaning] "novel," because it has been accepted by the very same theorists of poetics (*ālaṅkārikas*).
Locanā: (lo,

a) Now, wishing to dispel misconceptions regarding the two types of poetry just mentioned— which depend upon the establishment of the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*)— and commencing the first chapter, [the author] first presents [a verse] that refutes [the view that suggestion is] knowable through the ancient modes of signification such as direct denotation (*abhidhā*).
He introduces the first verse with "atha" (now).
What? That is, what is its authority?
This [verse] just mentioned is the proof for the two-fold division of poetry.

Abhinava—those who know the true essence of the meaning of the scriptures on poetics—[state that] a fourth function (*vṛtti*) must be accepted for the cognition of rasa and the like, which was not demonstrated by the teachers prior to the venerable teacher Ānandavardhana, the incarnation of the Poetic Person (*kāvyapuruṣa*). This [fourth function] pertains to the repose of the functions known as denotation (*abhidhā*), indication through intention (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*). (VisSd 5.1)
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the phrase "of the functions" (*vṛttīnām*), it refers to the three functions known as denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and intentionality (*tātparya*).
Regarding the phrase "due to cessation" (*vikṣānteḥ*), the meaning is: due to the desisting from [the process of] making known the object to be understood by oneself.
Turyā means the fourth.
Locanā:
Regarding "of the functions" (*vṛttīnām*)—the function that is the fourth is the object of designations such as "manifestation," "resounding," "movement," and "cognition."
By the word *rasa* (flavor), here, all that is to be tasted is intended;
by the word *ādi* (and so forth), both the matter (*vastu*) and the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) are included.
Because of the preeminence of *rasa*, it is mentioned first.

Direct denotation (*abhidhā*), which ceases once it has conveyed the merely conventional meaning, lacks the capacity to convey the suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) such as objects, poetic figures, and aesthetic flavors (*rasa*).
Furthermore, aesthetic flavor and the like are not conventionally denotable;
for the denotation of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth is not itself the denotation of that [flavor].
This is because its identity with that [sentiment] is not admitted.
Furthermore, we shall explain that where there is a designation by its own name, on the contrary, it is indeed a defect.
And in some cases, such as "this is the erotic sentiment" (*śṛṅgāraraso 'yam*), even though there is a designation by its own name, there is no cognition of that [sentiment].

Because its nature is self-luminous bliss (*svaprakāśānanda*). Furthermore, even the function (*vṛtti*) called "intentionality" (*tātparya*), which is accepted by the proponents of the theory of the connection of the expressed (*abhihitānvayavādin*), is exhausted merely in [conveying] the relation [between word-meanings] and does not bring about the cognition of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Vijñapriyā: [Commentary on the above].
He explains [the verse] with the words "of denotation" (*abhidhāyāḥ*).
Now, one might object: "Let rasa and so forth be understood by denotation itself. To this he replies: "And it is not conventional" (*na ca saṃketitaḥ*).

Again, one might argue: "Is it not the case that rasa, bhāva, and so forth are indeed conventionally established by the excitants (*vibhāva*) and the rest? To this he replies: "For it is not so" (*na hi*).
In that case, "identity" (aikyarūpya) means being of the same nature;
for the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth are the hero and others, while the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is the manifestation of those [excitants] and so on.
He states another objection to the denotation (*abhidhā*) of rasa when it is to be understood: "And where...
He says: "But in some cases... [meaning] that when words such as *rasa* and so forth are denoted as being part of poetry, there is no apprehension of rasa and the like.
Now, one might object: let rasa and the like not be conveyed by denotation; [let them be conveyed by suggestion].
To ensure that [the meaning] is understood through the function called *tātparya* (intentional import), which is accepted by the Naiyāyikas, he says: "according to the theory of *abhihitānvaya*.
*Locanā*:
The conventionalized meaning is the expressed (*vācya*) sense.
Anticipating the objection, "Why is *rasa* and so forth not also designated [by words]?", he says: "And not... He asks, "Why?
and says: "For... [If this were the case,] such would be the meaning.
If it is argued that rasa and the rest are denoted by convention, is this so by means of words expressing the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth,
or by their own specific words?
It cannot be the first, because those [rasas] are to be manifested by the excitants and the other factors.
Furthermore, if it were expressed by its own name, there would be no apprehension of it, but rather a fault;
for "its own name" means the word *rasa* or words such as *śṛṅgāra* and so forth.

And in such instances as, "O friend, in spring, the charming Hari plays like the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) personified," the manifestation of that [sentiment] arises solely from the totality of the excitants (vibhāva) and other factors, and not from the word "erotic" itself.
This means that it is through mere association that the meanings denoted by each individual word [contribute].

And as for what some say—"This [process] is like that of an arrow, an operation of denotation that is longer and longer still"—[the answer is: it is precisely the function (*vṛtti*), in the form of a power (*śakti*), which makes known the already established denoted meaning, that makes known the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). This is *Vijñapriyā* (vi, gha).

As for the opinion held by some that, just as an arrow released from the bow pierces one aimed target with a long-lasting activity in the form of velocity, and subsequently pierces another unaimed target as well with that very same activity of velocity which has become even longer [in duration], so it is here.

To refute the view of the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*— that it is only the function of *tātparya* (implication) that conveys the suggested meaning— he raises both points with the words "And as for some...":

regarding what has been stated by some that "it is *abhidhā* (denotation) itself in the form of 'this is that' which conveys the suggested meaning," the meaning is that it is like the operation of an arrow whose nature is the denotation "this is that."
Locanā:
(lo, ī) "And that which..."—this is the meaning: just as an arrow released by an archer pierces many things, such as an enemy's armor, by means of a single operation consisting of its momentum;
In the same way, the function of a single word extends as far as it brings about the cognition of its intended object (*uddeśya*).
As for what the creditor said: "Because suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is not distinct from intentionality (*tātparya*), there is no such thing as *dhvani*."
"Since it extends as far as the purpose to be accomplished, its intended meaning (tātparya) has not been weighed on a scale."
Thus [ends the objection]. *Vijñapriyā*:

As for the statement "and that which is called *dhvani*..."—namely, "because it is distinct from *tātparya* (intentional meaning)"—since the capacity to suggest (*vyañjakatva*) or the act of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is distinct from *tātparya*, this [suggestion] is neither *dhvani* nor *vyañjanā*.

But the meaning is simply *tātparya* (purport). To the extent that there is an action— namely, the function consisting of the communication of a meaning— it is *tātparya* because it extends over that [function].
The meaning is that it is not determined by weighing.
Locanā:
(lo, u) Dhvani is the author of the *Daśarūpaka*.
The intended effect is the objective, meaning that for whose sake the employment of words occurs; this is the sense.
It is not, however, held by a scale.
In some cases, having brought the proliferation [of thought] to a halt, it is established as being restricted solely to the cognition of the meaning of a sentence.
Regarding those two, the opponents themselves must apply the "stick" of the argument: "There is no functioning of words, cognitions, or actions after they have ceased.
(Vijñapriyā)
"Over those two" means over the proponents of the operation of the word (*iṣu-vyāpāra-vādin*) and the proponents of the intention (*tātparya-vādin*).
If there were an intention to convey both the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) meanings simultaneously, it would be logically impossible for them to be conveyed sequentially.
The meaning is that there would be an absence of activity after having ceased [the process] during the gradual awakening to its existence.
However, this objection is not convincing;
for even by the proponent of *vyañjanā* (manifestation), since gradual awakening is admitted, the occurrence of activity after having ceased is accepted.

If it is argued that when there is *tātparya* (intentional import), a difference in the modes of operation (*vṛtti*) itself is accepted as the "operation with a pause" (*viramya-vyāpāra*), and not by means of a single mode of operation, we say no;
for since *tātparya* alone is the regulating factor, the difference in the modes of operation is irrelevant.

And because there is equality regarding the cessation of sound in both cases, the fault lies in the absence of any factor that apprehends the intended meaning (*tātparya*) for those two, which occurs through gradual cognition. Nor should it be said that the result itself is what apprehends that [meaning];
Since the intended meaning (*tātparya*) occurs subsequent to the fruit [of the communication],
when there is a gradual awakening through *vyañjanā*, it is precisely the specificities of the speaker, the listener, and so forth, that serve as the indicators of the intended meaning.
And thus, let that very thing which is grasped by them be the function (*vṛtti*) of the intended meaning according to the view of Dhvani.

It should not be said that [the suggested meaning] is not the literal sense (*vyañjana*), because in the example "it is not the literal sense," the suggested erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which is not the intended object of the statement, is subordinate;

or as in the sentence "Eat fragrant meat," where the intention is "fragrant" (meaning *sugandhi*) meat, there is the suggestion of cow-meat. However, according to the view that maintains that the primary function of words is denotation (*abhidhā*), the very absence of a lexicon or other means to grasp that denotation is the defect.

The statement that the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is understood even without being grasped by the denotative function (*abhidhā*) is to be rejected precisely because there is no evidence for such a thing.
Locanā:

(Lo, Ū) This refers to those who maintain that there is no separate operation [of suggestion] once the word has ceased its activity—namely, the proponents of *abhihitānvaya* (those who hold that the connection of meanings occurs after they have been denoted).
The meaning is: "What business have we, as ginger merchants, with the concern for the ship?
And so, why should one abandon the primary denotation (*lakṣaṇā*)?
For even through the operation of expression (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) over a very long distance, the comprehension of that meaning is established.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, cha) Regarding the function (*vṛtti*) consisting of denotation (*abhidhā*) which conveys the expressed meaning, he states another defect in its capacity to convey the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), beginning with "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).
Locanā:
And thus, the sense is that if the entire meaning understood immediately after hearing a word is within the scope of that word’s primary denotation (*abhidhā*), then that is its function.
After the term "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*), the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) is to be supplied as a supplement; its meaning is that which is to be indicated (*lakṣaṇīya*).
And why is it that even in cases such as "O Brahmin, a son has been born to you" or "Your daughter is pregnant," joy, sorrow, and so forth are not considered the expressed meaning?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) [Objection: But surely metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must not be accepted at all; to this he says: "If it is asked why...
[He explains: "A maiden" means here, a maiden who has not been given away.

The meaning is as follows: because of the father's grief within her very womb; for here, since joy and sorrow are perceived in the brahmin immediately after hearing such words from another person present near him, it follows that those two [joy and sorrow] would have to be considered the expressed meanings (*vācya*) of those words themselves, given that their cognition is possible through the very long-lasting denotation (*abhidhā*) of those words.
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) He states another logical inconsistency with the words "If it is asked why...
The meaning is this: for joy and the other [emotions] are not accepted by anyone as being denotable [by words].
For these [words] do not produce [their effects] through the cognition of the expressed meaning;
indeed, a word does not possess the nature of a producer (*kāraka*), because it is a communicator (*jñāpaka*).
Furthermore, it has been stated: "Every sentence, whether of human origin or not of human origin, is directed toward an effect (*kārya*);
for if it were not so directed, it would be unworthy of acceptance, like the speech of a madman.

Consequently, since no purpose conducive to the activity of either the speaker or the listener is perceived in poetic words other than the tasting of unsurpassed pleasure, [the purpose] is indeed the tasting of unsurpassed pleasure."
"It is determined as the effect,
according to the maxim: 'Whatever a word aims at, that is the meaning of the word.'"—
Vijñapriyā.

(vi, jha) "Whatever a word aims at, that is its meaning"—this very statement of Jaimini is the authority for the function called *tātparya* (intentional focus) in the cognition of the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*). To refute this view, he raises [the following objection]: "As for that which...
refers to human worldly speech and non-human Vedic speech.

"Intent on the task" (kāryaparam) means having the goal of what is to be accomplished (sādhya) as its purport. Now, one might ask: "What follows from this intentness on the task in the present context? To this he says: "And therefore..."—namely, that the very savoring of unsurpassed bliss is experienced as the task to be accomplished.

And thus, the capacity of a poetic sentence to cause the relish of pleasure occurs precisely through the awakening of its suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), because this sentence has that suggested meaning as its intended purport (*tātparya*).
"That is the meaning of the word" means that the meaning of the word *sa* in the Jaimini-sūtra is the object obtained through the function of purport (*tātparyavṛtti*).

In the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, however, a different meaning is assigned to this statement. For it says: “That which is the primary object—that toward which a word has the intentionality of being something to be accomplished—is the meaning that determines the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of that word; but its authority does not reside in the established portion. For example, in the sentence “Bring the cow” (*gām abhyāja*), the factor to be accomplished—the act of bringing—is the meaning that determines the authority, and not the established portion, the cow; or as in: [the example continues].

In the injunction "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the curd possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*), and its role as an auxiliary part (*upādeyāṃśa*) is likewise established therein;
however, the aspect of the oblation (*homāṃśa*) is not established from another sentence. (Locanā)

Now, having raised a doubt regarding the view of a certain proponent of a specific school of the Guru-mata—who maintains that "the meaning of a word is that which the word aims at"—he refutes it with the words "But as for that which... (*yat punar...*).
The portion of the text ending with "...by the logic beginning with 'it is of human origin' (*pauruṣeya*)," etc., constitutes the statement of the objection.
The final position [siddhānta] begins with "In that regard" (tatra) and so forth.
Mundane [knowledge] is of human origin; Vedic [knowledge] is not of human origin.
The "task" (kārya) is the objective to be aimed at.
And therefore, the meaning is that inference is as follows:
the person to be instructed (*pratipādya*) is the one to whom the statement is addressed; the instructor (*pratipādaka*) is the one who causes it to be heard.
The meaning is that [the object] is determined as being the effect (kārya).

Therefore, the object consisting of the experience of unsurpassed bliss, in the form of rasa and so forth, becomes the intended referent (tātparya-viṣaya) of the word; what is the need for postulating another mode of operation (vṛttyantara)?
This is the position [of the author] which is employed with a specific purpose.
That meaning of a word must necessarily be understood by means of the word.
In this regard, it must be asked: what is this so-called "intentionality" (*tatparatva*), or is it "having that as its object" (*tadarthatva*)?
Or is it its capacity to convey that meaning through the function of *tātparya* (implied intention)?
In the first case, there is no dispute,
because even if [the meaning] is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), its status as the intended meaning (*tadarthatā*) is not lost.

Regarding the second [alternative], however: what is this function called *tātparya* (purport), which is accepted by the proponents of the theory of "the connection of what has been expressed" (*abhihitānvaya-vāda*), or is it something other than that?
In the first case, the answer has already been given.
But in the second case, there is a dispute over mere terminology,
for even in that view, a fourth function is established.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi ña) He reflects upon a meaning he has himself imagined: "In that regard, it must be asked. The meaning of the sentence "That is the word-meaning" is its *tatparatva* (being directed toward that). He asks about that very *tatparatva*: "What is this?
Its being for that purpose (*tadarthatva*) consists in having the cognition of that [object] as its aim.

"Because its purpose is not lost"—that is, because its function of producing that cognition is not lost. "The answer has already been given"—the meaning is that they admit the function called *tātparya* (purport) only with respect to the relation itself.

As for the phrase "or something else," the claim made by the proponent of *dhvani*—namely, that the function called *tātparya*, after making the relation known, also makes the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) known—has already been refuted.
The meaning of the phrase "or something else" (*tato 'nyā vā*) is simply that there is a distinct category of object (*atirikta-padārtha*) which is different from *tātparya*.
Regarding the claim that it is "merely a name": in the accepted fourth function (*turīya-vṛtti*), it is said, "Whether it be *vyañjanā* or *tātparya*, that is its name."
The meaning is that this is precisely the point of contention.
*Locanā*:
Regarding "therein"—the meaning is that one must inquire into what was stated [in the verse], beginning with "composed by a person" (*pauruṣeya*).
"Having that as its object" means that the word has that as its meaning.
An answer to this has already been given by the passage beginning with "of those two, above," and so forth.

Now, one might argue: "Let it be that the manifestation of the connection between the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, as well as the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, occurs simultaneously through the power of *tātparya* (implicatory function). If this is said:
No, because the relationship of cause and effect between those two is accepted;
as the Sage said: "The production of rasa results from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory states (vyabhicārin).
Furthermore, if they were simultaneous, how could there be a causal relationship even between the left and right horns of a cow?
Because of the reversal of the sequence [of the words].
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) But surely, the fourth function (*vṛtti*), which consists of a distinct category of meaning, is not mentioned by the author of the *Dhvani*?

However, it is only that which has a fixed (kḷpta) intentionality (*tātparya*) that conveys the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). And since that [intentionality] brings about understanding only in a sequential manner,

one raises the objection— starting with "But surely" (*nanu*)— that the previously stated refutation, namely that "words, cognitions, and actions [cannot occur simultaneously]," would apply here as well if the meaning were understood all at once.
"By the power of intentionality" means by the function consisting of intentionality.
"Of those two" refers to the manifestation of the connection between the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, and the manifestation of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the production of rasa," the production of rasa is indeed the production of its cognition, because that which is self-luminous is non-different from its own cognition.
And by the fifth [verse], the causality of the cognition of the connection between the negative correlate (*vibhāva*) and so forth is demonstrated.
By the phrase "and in the case of coexistence" (*sahabhāve ca*), he shows the non-arising of that causality which was demonstrated [to exist] when there is arising through coexistence— namely,
in the case of the left horn of a cow or the right horn of a rabbit, or the horns of a donkey, a deer, or an ox.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) "nanu" [is used] immediately after "prakāśanam" (manifestation).
"In that case, there would be no operation after [the word] has ceased," such is the remainder [of the argument].
By this very same line of reasoning, even in the case of objects (vastu) and poetic figures (alaṅkāra) which are being perceived,
the acceptance of suggestion (vyañjanā) is entirely untenable, based on the principle that "whatever a word aims at is its meaning."

Furthermore, for those who accept the maxim that "the meaning of a word is that which the word aims at," if they do not admit *vyañjanā* (suggestion), then in cases such as "the grove of *vānīra* reeds," what function's domain would the suggested meaning— which appears as subordinate yet is nonetheless perceived— occupy, given that the word does not aim at it?
In that case, would it not be like the Bhaṭṭa position, such as in the example: "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," [whereby one infers] "he eats at night"?

If it is argued that, as in such examples, one should likewise postulate a "remainder of the sentence" (*vākyaśeṣa*) for the perception of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) here as well, we say no. This is because of the maxim: "It is better to postulate a property (*dharma*) than to postulate a substratum (*dharmī*)," and thus it is more logical to postulate a distinct function (*vyāpāra*).

Furthermore, in cases such as "The hamlet is on the Ganges," how could indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which ceases once it has conveyed the mere meaning of the bank and so forth, possibly convey the suggested meanings of coolness, purity, and the like?
Therefore, it is beyond dispute that the fourth function (*vṛtti*) alone is to be cultivated.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭha) But surely, suggestion (*vyañjanā*) based on indication (*lakṣaṇā*) should not be respected?

[The opponent might argue: "Let both the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) and the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) be understood by means of a single indication (*lakṣaṇā*). To this, he says: "In the Gaṅgā...
Locanā:

(Lo, o) Having thus refuted the view that the aforementioned suggested meanings are conveyed by denotation (*abhidhā*) or intention (*tātparya*), he now refutes their being conveyed by indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with the words: "In the Gaṅgā..."
He summarizes with the words "by that": by that cause.
Furthermore—

The suggested meaning differs from the expressed meaning due to the differences in the cognizer, the nature [of the cognition], number, cause, effect, time of comprehension, locus, object, and so forth. (VisSd 5.2)
Vijñapriyā: (vi,

ḍa) But surely, since direct denotation (*abhidhā*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*) have already become extended enough to convey the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), why should there be a cessation of those two?

In your view, the operation of a word that occurs after it has ceased [its primary function] must be accepted just as it is in the case of the communication of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*); therefore, he establishes the difference between the operation that communicates the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and the operation that communicates the suggested meaning precisely through this dissimilarity.
Furthermore—regarding the phrase "the nature of the cognizer" (*boddhṛ-svarūpa*)—"cognizer" (*boddhā*), "nature" (*svarūpa*),...
Number,
cause,
and effect.
Cognition, time, and the substratum.
The meaning is that there is a distinction between [the functions of] *viṣaya* (object) and so forth.
He himself will demonstrate this distinction later:

"The suggested (*vyaṅgya*) is distinct from the denoted (*abhidheya*)."—although it is precisely the distinction between *abhidhā* (denotation) and *vyañjanā* (suggestion) that ought to be demonstrated.
Nevertheless, with the intention that by demonstrating the distinction between those two, the distinction of that which makes them known is also demonstrated, it was stated in this way.
*Locanā*:
(Lo, Au) He introduces another objection regarding the suggestible being the denoted meaning, beginning with "furthermore" (*kiñca*).
The term "due to difference" (bhedāt) is to be construed with each [term] beginning with "the cognizer" (boddhṛ); thus, due to the difference between cognizers,
and due to the difference in intrinsic nature (svarūpa).

The phrase "due to the difference in number" (*saṃkhyābhedāt*) and so forth is to be understood as follows: there is indeed a distinction between the cognizers because the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) are perceived respectively by grammarians—who are skilled in the knowledge of words and their meanings alone—and by connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). *Vijñapriyā*: [This is the commentary on the aforementioned point.]
(vi, ḍha) Therein, he demonstrates the distinction between the perceivers: "of the expressed meaning and the suggested meaning.
The connection is according to the respective order: that the expressed meaning is perceived by grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), and the suggested meaning by connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).

For grammarians are indeed skilled only in the knowledge of a word and the meaning expressed by that word, but not in the knowledge of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*). [As in the verse: “O pious man, wander away... (p. 242).

In such cases, there is a distinction in essential nature: in some instances where the expressed meaning is positive, it takes the form of a negation; and in others, such as "The sandalwood paste has completely vanished... (verse 62), where the expressed meaning is negative, it takes the form of an affirmation.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) He shows the distinction in their essential natures with the word "bhrama" (whirling). Here, the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is the injunction to whirl.
Non-going is the negation that is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Regarding the phrase "in the form of a negation": the non-going to his presence is the expressed (*vācya*) negation;
the meaning is that the injunction to go to his presence is the suggested sense.
The meaning is that when the affirmative form (*vidhirūpa*) is expressed and known, the negative form (*niṣedharūpa*) is understood as the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
The same applies in subsequent cases as well.
— *Locanā*:
In passages such as "niḥśeṣacyutacandanam," having accepted that the meaning "she has gone" (*gatāsīt*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), its description as being of a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) is made.
And in cases such as "gato 'stakarkaḥ," only a single expressed meaning (*vācya-artha*) is perceived.

The suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), however, due to the difference between the cognizer and others, is in some cases: "Go to meet your lover," "Let the cows be penned up," or "This is the time for the hero's arrival."
The distinction of number is manifold, such as in the form "there is no longer any distress" and so forth.
Locanā:
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "the cognizer, etc.," the speaker, the context, and so on are included.

The expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is to be known merely by the utterance of words, whereas this [suggested meaning] is known through such factors as the purity of one's creative intuition (*pratibhā*); thus, there is a difference in their causes.
Furthermore, there is a difference in their effects: the former produces mere cognition, while the latter produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) He shows the distinction in number—namely, "the expressed meaning" (*vācyārtha*).
"This" means the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).

He demonstrates the difference in their functions: "merely the cognition of the denoted" means that the function of denotation (*abhidhā*) is merely the cognition of the denoted object (*abhidheya*), whereas the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is also aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
Thus, there is a distinction between the two cognitions based on their being merely formal and their being characterized by aesthetic wonder.
There is a difference in time by way of priority and posteriority;
and there is a difference in substratum by way of being the substratum of sound, as well as the substratum of words, their parts, their meanings, phonemes, and syntactical arrangements.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, tha) It demonstrates the difference in time with the words "before and after.
It demonstrates the difference in substratum with the words "as having sound as its substratum.
The substratum of denotation is sound alone.
As for *vyañjanā*, it consists of words, parts of words, phonemes (*varṇa*), and so forth. For example:
“Who would not feel anger upon seeing the bitten lip of his beloved, who is perverse in forbidding [him] while she smells a lotus full of bees? Suffer this now! (Gāthāsaptaśatī 6.45)
Thus, there is a distinction of objects based on whether they concern a female friend or her lover.
Therefore, that which is suggested (vyaṅgya) is not merely the expressed meaning (abhidheya).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) He demonstrates the distinction of the object: "kassa vā ṇa hoi" ("To whom would it not happen?").
To whom would anger not arise upon seeing the wounded lip of one's beloved?
[This applies] to one who is smelling a lotus with bees clinging to it.
"Vārita-vāme!
Sahasva idānīm!
Thus is the Sanskrit.

This is the deceptive speech of the heroine’s friend directed toward her husband, who is threatening his wife whose lower lip has been bitten by a paramour. "O you who are stubborn despite being forbidden!"—
on the surface, this means "O you who are perverse and obstinate when forbidden from smelling the lotus with its bee."
"In the case of 'vāma' [left], it refers to the act of biting the lower lip up to the limit of the restraint during sexual intercourse"; this, however, is a hidden meaning.
In the phrase "sahasva" (endure), the husband's act of threatening should be understood.
Regarding the phrase "the friend and her beloved": the "friend" is the heroine (nāyikā) who speaks, and "her beloved" is her husband.
"By virtue of being its object" means by virtue of being the object of that [speaker's] cognition.
For by the heroine, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha) is understood as "she is deceiving me.
Therefore—the meaning is that the suggested meaning is not accessible through denotation (abhidhā).
—Locanā:

(Lo, i) "Or whose is this?"—referring to her who has turned away from her purpose toward the left, acting in opposition; in that case, the statement concerning the female friend is: "Her lip has been bitten by a bee."
"But not by one who desires another"—
this suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), however, refers to the beloved.

Thus, the intention is that if there were identity between the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) despite differences in the nature of the cognizer and so forth, then there would be no distinction anywhere, such as between blue and yellow, or between a man and a bull.

If it is objected: "In a sentence such as 'The sun has set,' how can the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha)—such as 'Go to meet your lover'—be cognizable through the authority of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*), given that it is understood only with the assistance of other indicators like context (*prakaraṇa*) and the like, and thus lacks the quality of being cognizable by verbal testimony alone?

To this, some say: Just as when there is a desire to know whether a certain expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) conveyed by words is true or false, its truth becomes an object of inference, the domains of the two means of knowledge—verbal testimony and inference—are distinct.

However, since that which is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) is understood through verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, there is a disparity between the example and the case to be illustrated.
If it is asked, "What then is the resolution in that regard?"—the connection is as follows:
just as context and the like serve to delimit the denotation of Viṣṇu and other referents even when they are multiple, so too does it function for that which has multiple suggestors (*vyañjaka*).

In the case of a word having a single suggested meaning (*ekavyaṅgya*), the assistance provided by context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors constitutes the "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*); thus, it is established by logic that the word is subordinate (*aṅga*) and its own subordinate elements do not create an intervention. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the authority of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*). And here, although after the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), when one desires to investigate whether it is true or false, its truth is understood through another means of knowledge—namely, inference alone—[nevertheless...]

Nevertheless, because there is no absence of valid cognition regarding the meaning of the sentence—which was already established prior to the inquiry into its truth or falsity—and because it is cognizable solely through verbal testimony, there is no contradiction of the authority of the word (*śabda*).
For the perceptual authority [of the senses] is not contradicted when the truth or falsity of what is perceived by the eye and other organs is subsequently investigated.
Likewise—
Locanā: (lo, ī) "So be it.
Indeed, it is not the case that suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) lack the status of being understood through denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or suggestion (*bodhya*).
Rather, the meaning is "even otherwise.
Since taste and so forth do not exist previously, the two—indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and denotation (*abhidhā*)—are the means of their cognition;
furthermore, indication occurs even in the absence of any sublation of the primary meaning. (VisSd 5.3)
The ellipsis is "not indicative of [the taste] and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā* explains: since neither indication (*lakṣaṇā*) nor direct denotation (*abhidhā*) is possible for that which indicates taste and so forth, he says: "because it did not exist previously."

Since the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the words contained in that poem is produced only immediately after the verbal cognition (*śabdabodha*), it does not exist prior to that [cognition]; therefore, it is impossible for the apprehension of those two—*śakti* (denotative power) or *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function)—to occur with respect to that [flavor], because they can only be grasped with respect to an object already present at the time.

If it is argued: "Let there be the apprehension of *śakti* even with respect to a future *rasa*, which is yet to be experienced, by means of a 'universal indication' (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) consisting of a general property residing in that *rasa* which is being experienced for the first time from the poem," we say no.

It should also be understood that this [recognition of rasa] is possible only through primary denotation (śakti) or indication (lakṣaṇā), because the rasa is not present prior [to the apprehension of the excitants, etc.], and because the words denoting the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth lack the capacity to convey that [rasa].
Nor can there be such an apprehension from words like "śṛṅgāra" occurring in poetry, even if they possess a conventionally established denotative power (śakti) acquired through lexicons (koṣa).
Because it is not experienced [as such];
on the contrary, if it did exist, the fault of rasa and so forth being denotable by their own words would be stated later.
Therefore, if it were not cognizable by words such as "erotic" (*śṛṅgāra*) and so on, it would fail to attain the status of being *rasa*.

However, since that [rasa] is perceived only through the medium of the expression of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, its apprehension is based on experience. Now, one might object: "In this case, since rasa and the like have already been presented by the words 'erotic' (*śṛṅgāra*) and so on, let there be a cognition of rasa and the like through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of the words expressing the excitants and so forth.
To this, he says: "Furthermore, regarding the primary meaning... (*kiñca mukhyārtha...*).
Regarding the word *lakṣaṇā*, he appends the remainder of the phrase from the preceding section—"not by means of awakening"—to it.
Locanā:
"Previously."
The meaning is this: since the suggested meanings such as rasa and bhāva do not exist prior [to the cognition], neither indication (lakṣaṇā) nor denotation (abhidhā) can be their means of cognition.
Furthermore, because all three types of suggested meanings lack the sublation of the primary meaning (mukhyārthabādha), indication cannot be their means of cognition either.
The particle "api" is used for the purpose of conjunction with what was stated previously.

Indeed, there exists no entity established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) that is distinct from the operation consisting of aesthetic relish (rasanā) and yet is denotable by words such as "rasa" (aesthetic flavor), which these two [theories of] indication (lakṣaṇā) and designation (abhidhā) might convey.

Furthermore, it is only in cases such as "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā," where the intended syntactic connection (anvaya) of the meanings expressed by the uttered words is obstructed by its impossibility, that indication (lakṣaṇā) finds its scope.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, na) [Objection: But surely, since there is an intention (*tātparya*) toward rasa as well, the very fact that it cannot be established without indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is what is called "sublation of the primary meaning" (*mukhyārthabādha*). To this he says: "For not... If the rasa and so forth were already present prior to the word [denoting them], only then would the aforementioned sublation of the primary meaning be defined for the sake of understanding that [rasa] through indication; but that is not the case here. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that the object to be conveyed by rasa and so forth is indeed distinct from such rasa itself— [rasa] being that whose function consists of both the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the suggestiveness (*vyañjanā*).
"Desiring to become" (*bubhūṣan*) means wishing to come into existence.
The persistence of sound and so forth in a stream and such [is established];
Locanā:
(lo, ū) immediately after [the statement] "not established by valid cognition,"...
The word "somewhere" (*kvacid*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
As it was stated by the teacher Udayana in the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*:
"For a sentence that has no further expectancy because its connection with what has been heard is complete does not require another [sentence]."
"Because of the absence of a connection between the word-meanings, there is a relation with that which is implied by them."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) He shows the agreement regarding this point by saying "it has been stated":
"from the connection with what was heard"—that is, because the connection between the words and their meanings as they were heard is possible.

For a sentence that is uncontradicted and lacks expectancy toward anything else does not desire nor expect another [sentence], because of the deficiency in the syntactic connection of word-meanings— that is, because a connection between the two word-meanings is impossible.
"By that which is implied" means by that which is indicated.
"Connection" (*saṅgati*) means "logical sequence" (*anvaya*).
Locanā:
[This refers to] "due to the logical sequence of what has been heard" (*śrutānvayāt*).
"Anything else" means another category of entity (*padārthāntara*).
He does not desire it, nor does he require it.
However, in the case of "a hamlet on the Ganges," [the situation is different].

In such cases, at the very time of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the word-meanings, the connection is obstructed by the manifestation of a contradiction (*bādha*). Therefore, the meaning is that there is no "conjunction" (*saṅgati*), which is to say *anvaya*, with that bank or other object implied by the word-meaning such as "consisting of water";
this is not the case, however, in instances such as "The bedchamber is empty... (p. 22).
The contradiction with the literal meaning [is as follows]:
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) Thus, "the dwelling house is empty."

In passages such as these, because the connection with the observation of empty dwellings and so forth is not contradicted, there is no definition of rasa; thus he says, "but not," [in the phrase] "na punar" (Locanā:
lo, ṝ). To the question "What follows from that?", he replies: "but not."
The meaning is: how then could there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the cognition of rasa and so forth?

Furthermore, if in examples such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" the purpose were the indicated object, then the bank would have to be the primary meaning and [the literal sense] would have to be sublated.

Furthermore, since that [suggestion] would also be an object of indication (*lakṣya*), there would be another purpose for it, and yet another purpose for that as well, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
[Vijñapriyā:
But surely, in this way, let *vyañjanā* (suggestion) be accepted solely for the sake of bringing about the apprehension of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Regarding the statement that coolness and purity are suggested in such cases as "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā," let there be only indication (lakṣaṇā) even there, following the indication of the bank; what is the need for suggestion (vyañjanā)?
Thus he says: "And if...
The "purpose" (prayojana) is that which is not the object of the knowledge that constitutes the purpose.
The phrase "there would be both primacy of meaning and contradiction" implies that neither of these two actually exists.
If the purpose (*prayojana*) were itself to be defined, there would be an infinite regress; therefore, he says: "of that too" (*tasyāpi*).
Regarding the phrase "because of the fall into infinite regress," the meaning is "and because of the fall into infinite regress. — *Locanā*

(Lo, Ḷ) One might object: "In that case, let there be no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in *dhvani* where the intended meaning is not the literal one; however, in *dhvani* where the literal meaning is not intended, a purpose (*prayojana*) consisting of qualities such as coolness and purity must indeed be indicated. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And if... For a word, having first conveyed its primary meaning, indicates a related meaning when that [primary] meaning cannot cohere with the sentence-meaning.
In this context, if one were to perceive the purpose (prayojana) to be indicated immediately after the cognition of the bank, then the bank would be the primary meaning of the word "Ganges";
and in that case, there would be an impossibility of its connection with the sentence-meaning—this is the sense.
He states "of that too" to show that if the purpose itself were what is indicated, there would also be the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā).

The meaning is that for that [secondary sense] which is to be accepted by virtue of being "to-be-cut" (*takṣyatā*), there must be another purpose; for in the absence of a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or a specific purpose (*prayojana*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is impossible.
"Of that too" refers to the second purpose.

"An infinite regress that causes the destruction of the root"—here, the "root" refers to the acceptance, as the object of indication (*lakṣya*), of both the bank and the sanctity (*pāvanatva*) which is not [inherently] present in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The sense is that it is logical to abandon such a root of misfortune.
Furthermore, there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the bank as qualified by the purpose (*prayojana*).
Because it is not accepted that the object and the purpose are perceived simultaneously;
for it is only immediately after the cognition of blue and so forth that there can arise either the state of being known (*jñātatā*) or the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(Vi, Bha) [Objection: If there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the purpose (*prayojana*) only after the comprehension of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, let the indication be directed precisely toward the bank qualified by the purpose, as in "the hamlet on the cool and purifying bank. To this, he says: "And not even... In this context, one should keep in mind the "purpose" as stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: that the purpose is the cognition of a meaning in addition to what is expressed by the phrase "the hamlet on the Ganges bank."
He explains: "Of the object and the purpose.
For, when there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the bank as qualified by sanctity, the object of the indication is the bank, while the qualification is sanctity and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: the purpose (*prayojana*) consists in the simultaneous cognition of both [the primary meaning and the secondary meaning], such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*), which is the object of the cognition that serves as the purpose;
whereas in *lakṣaṇā* (indication), there is only the cognition of one [of these].
This is because [the simultaneous cognition] is not accepted [in the case of indication].

If it is asked, "What is the reason for not accepting that [direct denotation]?"—the reason is precisely the consequence of the non-difference between cause and effect; for, by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), the knowledge characterized by sanctity (*pāvanatva*) which is to be produced is nothing other than the very knowledge that serves as its purpose. Thus, this applies everywhere.
He states that a distinction between these two is indeed observed: "nīlādi" etc.
Knowledge of blue and so forth, in the form of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), is the cause; its effect, however, is "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*).
In the view of the Naiyāyikas and Murāri, the meaning is that there is a subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), and that such cause and effect arise only in succession;
furthermore, the meaning is that there is a distinction between these two successive [cognitions].
— *Locanā*:

(Lo, e) Now, if it is argued that the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must be resorted to in order to convey meanings such as the riverbank, then in this case let indication itself convey the bank as qualified by that [identity]; what is the need for another function?
For instance, the cognition of the bank through identity with the Gaṅgā is indeed the object indicated (*lakṣya*).

Anticipating the objection that the coolness and other qualities of the riverbank are already established by nature through the cognition of its identity with the Ganges, he says: "Nor even..."—the meaning is: "even when the indication (lakṣaṇā) is qualified by a purpose.
Why? He says:
"Inference is not capable of making known the suggested meanings such as rasa and the like."
Because the causes are merely appearances, there is no memory [of them], nor is there cognition of taste and so forth.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) According to the view of the author of the *Vyaktiviveka*, rasa is simply the inference of love (*rati*) and so forth from the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors;
it is not the manifestation (*vyañjanā*) of love and so forth.
He refutes that [position] with the words "not inference" (nānumānam).

The meaning is that inference is not capable of being the cause of cognition for the manifestation of rasa and so forth, which are the suggested meanings (vyaṅgya) such as love (rati) and the like. Why? To this he says: "because of its fallacious nature" (ābhāsatvena).

For according to the author’s view, even though it is possible for the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors when being cognized to serve as marks (*liṅga*) for [the inference of] passion (*rati*) and so forth,

the inferential cognition— "Rāma possesses passion directed toward Sītā, because he possesses the excitants such as Sītā"— is not *rasa*, because, lacking the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), it cannot be relished.

However, when the emotion such as love (rati) and so forth— which follows the positive and negative concomitance of words— is manifested by suggestion (*vyañjanā*), is meditated upon by the sensitive connoisseurs (*bhāvikas*), and is transformed into the nature of self-luminous bliss while being relished,
it is called *rasa*. And its status as something suggested is according to the analogy of the flavor of a mixed beverage (*prapānakarasa*).
Or rather, it is because the *rati* (erotic sentiment) and so forth that have entered into that body are themselves the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) meaning.

Thus, since the causes of such a *rasa*—namely, the *vibhāvas* and others which consist of the effects, causes, and auxiliary factors of *rati* and so forth—are merely semblances (*ābhāsa*), there is neither inference nor an inferential cognition; this is the meaning.

For instance, the *vibhāvas* and so forth, such as Sītā and the like, are causes residing in Rāma and others by virtue of their connection with the desire to see [her] and so on, which is the frequentative sense (*mūrtubartha*).

The *sādhya* (the thing to be proven), namely the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) as previously described, resides in the cognizer of the poem; therefore, the reasons [adduced] are either contradictory or unestablished, and thus constitute fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
This same point will also become clear in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
He states that the cognition of *rasa* and so forth is not even of the nature of memory: "And the cognition of *rasa* and so forth is not memory."

Some say that because it is produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the cognition of flavor and so forth is of the nature of memory (*smṛti*). However, this is merely an appearance, as it will be explained later that such a claim is subject to the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) which is also produced by mental impressions. In reality, however, [the cognition of flavor] is not memory, precisely because its nature is self-luminous bliss (*svaprakāśānanda*).
Because that very [suggestion] lacks such a state of being.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) Thus, having refuted the notion that this suggested meaning is something previously known, Mahimabhaṭṭa indeed [addresses] those things that suggest rasa, plot-matter, and poetic figures...

The inference that was presented for the purpose of subsuming [theories of] sentences has been rendered defective by the fault of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). For the author of the *Vyaktiviveka* states: “Even that cognition of rasa and so forth which arises from the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors must be included within inference itself;
for the cognition of the excitants, ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) is held to be the means of proving the cognition of rasa and so forth.”

For those [factors], having become the causes, effects, and auxiliary conditions for states such as love (*rati*), bring about the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) precisely by making them inferable; these very factors, when being perceived and having reached the state of relish, are called "flavors" (*rasa*).
Thus, the sequence of their perception is necessarily present, though it is not noticed merely because it occurs so rapidly.
Regarding what was stated, "since this process of manifestation continues even today," *Vijñapriyā* explains:
"by the author of the *Vyaktiviveka*."
The phrase "culminating in rasa and so forth" means having rasa and so forth as its object;
however, in some places the reading is "of rasa and so forth.
The meaning is that such a cognition [of rasa] is established from the excitants (vibhāva) and the other factors.
He explains the manner of their production by stating, "those very [elements]" (*ta eva*).

The meaning is that those very [mental states] such as love (*rati*) and so forth, when being inferred, reach the state of being relished (*āsvādya*) through repeated cultivation; thus, by means of a connection with cognition, they attain the status of *rasa* residing in the spectator (*sāmājika*).
As for the sequence of their perception (*tatpratītikrama*): it is the cognition of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
The meaning is that this is the sequence of realization: first, the inferential cognition of delight; then, repeated cultivation; and finally, aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*).
Regarding the phrase "due to being unaccustomed":

the meaning is that because the sequence of inference—dependent on the presence of [the emotions] such as sorrow and so forth—is not established due to the lack of habituation to the immediate succession of the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and other factors following the inference of love (*rati*) and so on, [the sequence] is not perceived.
However, he states "for even today" to show that the error arises from thinking that love and the rest are manifested by the *vibhāvas* and other factors alone.

In this regard, it must be asked: do you intend by "rasa" (aesthetic flavor) merely the knowledge of passion and so forth residing in Rāma and others, which is inferred from the cognition of the *vibhāvas* (determinants) and other factors presented through verbal expression and dramatic gesture;
or is it the self-luminous bliss (*svaprakāśānanda*) being cultivated by the spectators (*bhāvakas*) through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of that [knowledge]?
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding "through words and gestures" (*śabdābhinayaiḥ*): "words" (*śabda*) refers to the words that express the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth;
"gestures" (*abhinaya*) refers to dramatic performance (*nāṭyābhinaya*); and "communication" (*samarpaṇa*) means making [the meaning] known.
Passion (*rāga*) is attachment (*anurāga*), which is delight (*rati*).
The word "that" (*tad*) refers to what has already been shown previously.
In the phrase "or self-luminous bliss," the word "inference" (*anumiti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Because it is precisely the object of inferential cognition (*anumiti*) that is being deliberated upon.
Regarding the first [alternative], there is no dispute;
however, the distinction is simply this: "We do not designate the cognition of redness and so forth residing in Rāma and others by the name 'rasa'."

But the second [reason] is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) due to the absence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). [Thus,] there is no dispute. *Vijñapriyā*: (vi, la) "There is no dispute."
The meaning is that there is no dispute at first sight regarding whether the manifestation (*vyañjanā*) of love and so forth constitutes inference (*anumāna*).
A dispute would arise here only if the manifestation of love and so forth residing in Rāma and others were stated by me to be *rasa*;
however, that is not the case, as he says with the words "but rather" (*kiṃtu*).
It may be said that there is the manifestation (*vyañjana*) of love and so forth residing in Rāma and others;

and thus, the very love and so forth that is manifested—which is apprehended as non-different from the love and so forth of the audience members and is being savored through the operation called *rasanā*—is *rasa*. This is the established doctrine stated in the introduction to the definition of *rasa*. That itself is the second position.
He states that its being an object of inference is impossible, saying "But the second... [is not].
"Because of the absence of the apprehension of pervasion" means that in the case of a contradictory reason (*viruddhahetu*), there is a necessary presence of that [contradiction]; this is the sense.
It should also be understood that this is an elliptical indication for the reason of being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*).

The state of possessing excitants (*vibhāva*) such as Sītā and so forth resides only in Rāma and others, but not in the spectator (*sāmājika*). He states that this is merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*) by means of the word "because of the cause" (*hetoḥ*).
The second alternative for the term "unestablished" (*asiddha*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
This is the explanation of the phrase "by way of the fallaciousness of the reasons" (*hetūnām ābhāsatvena*).
*Locanā*:
"By way of the fallaciousness of the reason" (*hetor ābhāsatayā*) means "by way of the fallaciousness of the reasons."
Such is the meaning of the terms in the verse.
To explain how there is the fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), he says: "because of the absence of the apprehension of pervasion" (*vyāptigrahaṇābhāvāt*).
And as it was stated by that very same [author]:

“Wherever there is the mention or the dramatic representation of such excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), involuntary states (*sāttvika*), and transitory emotions (*sañcārin*), there the manifestation of the erotic and other sentiments occurs”— thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) are easily grasped.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, va) The author of the *Vyaktiviveka* establishes that the specific relations, qualifiers, and excitants (*vibhāva*), etc., as previously described, possess the property of being pervaded by the nature of bliss and the property of residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
To refute this, he raises that very point, saying: "As for what was said...
The phrase "of the involuntary (*sāttvika*) and transitory (*saṃcārī*) [emotions]" is stated with the intention of inferring the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
This is because, for them, only the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is the pervaded [element].

In some places, however, the reading is simply "of the determinants, consequents, and transitory states" (*vibhāvānubhāvasaṃcāriṇām*), and not "together with the involuntary states" (*sāttvikaiḥ*) and so forth.
"Denotation" (*abhidhāna*) refers to the expressive word.
In drama, there is the denotable object (*abhidheya*) and the action that manifests it;

both of these, by virtue of their relation as the basis for the cognition of their respective objects, reside in the spectator who is the locus of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). This is the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The meaning is that the state of being a half-pakṣa is easily grasped.
Locanā:
(lo, au) Here, having refuted the pervasion (*vyāpti*) shown by Mahimabhaṭṭa, he confirms the absence of the apprehension of pervasion with the words beginning "And that which... (*yacceti*).
By the phrase ending with "pakṣadharmatā" [the definition is established].
Therefore, from this, the manifestation of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) occurs; such is its form.
By that—
“That very collection of factors which you accept as the basis for the manifestation of another meaning is,
in our view, accepted as the means of cognition in the case of inference.”
Thus [it is said].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, śa) states this verse regarding it: "That which [occurs] in another object... and so forth.

The meaning is this: that very collection (*sāmagrī*) consisting of the *vibhāvas* and so forth, which you accept as the cause for the manifestation and aesthetic relish (*āsvādana*) of rasa—which is a distinct entity—is itself accepted by us as the means of cognition (*gamaka*), that is, as the inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*). — *Locanā*.
"You yourselves must seek such a pervasion (*vyāpti*); therefore, he says: *yārtha*.
The meaning is: that very collection of causes (*sāmagrī*) which is accepted as the cause for the manifestation of another object is, for us, the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
For even when the collection of causes is present, in the cognition of the manifested object, whatever [cause] arises from any source whatsoever, that alone is what is perceived.

Thus, in order to manifest the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), a logical mark (*liṅga*) must necessarily be sought; for without the apprehension of its pervasion (*vyāpti*), that [mark] would be nothing but a fallacy. Therefore, the point is that even for you, the cognition of the suggested meaning is not possible without the apprehension of pervasion.
Regarding the word *iti* in the phrase *sammateti*, it is to be connected with the phrase *yaccoktam*.

This too is not contradictory for us. For we do not intend such a cognition to be [an object] characterized by being tasted; rather, it is one that rests solely in self-luminosity and is filled with intense bliss.
Therefore, because this proves a different object from the object intended to be proven, the reason is fallacious.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṣa) He refutes this with the words "this too," meaning that inference is not of the nature of self-luminous bliss.
"Abounding" means having that very nature; the meaning is that it is precisely such a thing as is intended to be proven (*siṣādhayiṣita*).
And here, "being intended to be proven" is merely the state of being an object of desire.
But it is not the state of being intended to be inferred (*anumitsitatva*), because there is no inference regarding taste (*rasa*).
"Fallaciousness" (*ābhāsatā*) refers to the fallacious nature consisting of the unestablished reason (*asiddha*) and the redundant reason (*siddhasādhana*).
This objection has been stated merely for the sake of ease;
in reality, however, the self-luminous bliss being directly experienced by the audience is certainly not inferred,
because there is no desire to infer it (*anumitsā*).
For in his case, there is no necessary desire to infer [the rasa], whereas the cognition of the flavor (rasa) occurs necessarily.

Likewise, it should be understood that the causal complex consisting of the cognized excitants (vibhāva) and so forth exists even for a person who does not perceive the flavor; thus, there is a logical deviation (vyabhicāra).
Locanā:
(Lo, ā) He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "this too" (*idam api*).
This refers to what was just mentioned by Mahimabhaṭṭa.
The object intended to be established is the inclusion of rasa and so forth within inference;
this is another point already established.
In that regard, the state of being inferable belongs to the cognition that "there is the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and other rasas in this poem."
And as for the object suggested in the passage beginning with "O righteous one of mine" (p. 242):
"With his hand, restless during the water-sport, having released and then again covered the face of Rādhikā..."
May Kṛṣṇa, who delights in the separation and reunion of the pair of Cakravāka birds, protect the world.
In such cases as these, poetic figures like *rūpaka* (metaphor) and others are indeed only inferable (*anumeya*).

[The author] raises the following objection in order to refute the Naiyāyika position—that where there is suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of either a fact (*vastu*) or a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), that fact or figure is accessible only through inference (*anumāna-gamya*)—with the words "As for that which... (*yacceti*).
"And that which concludes" is connected with "far away" (dūreṇa).
"Has been stated" (*uktam*) is its supplement.
Thus, the meaning is: "and that which has been stated as concluding."
The implied object is the absence of wandering.
He shows the locus for the suggestion of an ornament with the words "during water-sports."
During their water-sports, Śrī Kṛṣṇa repeatedly splashes the moon-like face of Rādhikā with water from his own hand, and then covers it and uncovers it with that same hand.
Consequently, by the covering and uncovering of that moon, the union and separation of the pair of cakravāka birds occur;
when it is covered, the bird, being separated at night, experiences a sense of reunion due to the delusion that it is dawn.
The loosening [of the knot] occurs because of the delusion that it was the time of twilight characterized by the rising of the moon;
this is merely a description of Kṛṣṇa’s such curiosity.
As for the opening of the covering, it was done by Kṛṣṇa’s hand alone, and not by Rādhikā’s.

Because, when the hand engaged in that [action] is agitated by water-sports, it is possible for Kṛṣṇa’s own face alone to be splashed; therefore, it is impossible for his own face to be used for the purpose of covering [the other].

Alternatively—since, by means of Rādhikā, even the covering and the releasing are brought about through the sprinkling of water as performed by Kṛṣṇa’s hand, the covering and releasing are effected by that very hand which has been drawn [toward her] through her mediation.
In such cases, there are figures of speech (alaṃkāras) such as metaphor (rūpaka), and so forth.
In this verse, the meaning is that while there is the metaphorical identification of the face with the moon, another poetic figure arises from the two initial words in the subsequent verse.
Locanā:

(Lo, i) Having thus established that rasa and the like are not within the scope of inference, he demonstrates the same for the suggested *vastu* (fact) and *alaṅkāra* (figure) as well, beginning with "yacca."
The particle *ca* serves as a conjunction for what was stated previously.
In the phrase "paryavasyati," there is a connection with the word *iti*, which stands at a distance [from it].
The meaning is that what was stated by Mahimabhaṭṭa is also incorrect.
To the question "What was said?", he replies with the verse beginning "jalakelī" (in the water-sports).
In the passage beginning with "jalakelī," there is the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor).

Because the face of Rādhikā is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) as being the moon, when the moon is seen or not seen, the two *cakravāka* birds experience the perception of the presence or absence of night, which results in their union or separation.

To explain: "Inference is the cognition of the probandum (liṅgin) from the mark (liṅga), which is qualified by its presence in the subject (pakṣa), its presence in similar instances (sapakṣa), and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
[Vijñapriyā] (vi, ha):
Having introduced the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) as a real entity (vasturūpa), he establishes its status as an object of inference (anumeyatā) with the words "To explain" (tathā hi).
Knowledge regarding the object to be proven, which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*).
Locanā:
(lo, ī) He asks, "In what way is it to be inferred? and says, "For instance" (*tathāhi*).
The word "nāma" is used in the sense of manifestation.

[The definition consists in] the absence [of the reason] from the subject (*pakṣa*), such as a mountain and so forth; from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as a kitchen and so forth; and from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as a lake and so forth.
From the mark (*liṅga*), that is, the pervaded (*vyāpya*) such as smoke and so forth, [one infers] the marked (*liṅgin*), that is, the pervader (*vyāpaka*) such as fire and so forth.
Furthermore, an object that is unrelated to the expressed meaning is not cognized;
otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Therefore, there must indeed be some relationship between the two objects—the signified and the signifier.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) Since the three-fold nature of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is possible only when there is pervasion by the probandum (*sādhya*) and its presence [in the subject],
he shows them [the three forms] with the words "therefore" (*tataśca*).
A non-connection is non-pervasive;
because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), there would follow the cognition even of that which is not a pervader.
A certain connection, however, takes the form of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Locanā:
(lo, u) In this context, [the phrase] "O righteous man, wander about! [is used].
In such cases, the object of cognition is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), while the cognizer is the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
Consequently, the cognizing meaning is the logical mark (*liṅga*), and the object of cognition is the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
Furthermore, the presence of the meaning that serves as the indicator (bodhaka) in the subject (pakṣa) is indeed explicitly stated;
while its presence in similar instances (sapakṣa) and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) are not explicitly stated, they are to be understood through implication.

Therefore, in this case, the comprehension of the indicated meaning (vyaṅgyārtha), which is the object possessing the mark (liṅgin), from the expressed meaning that serves as the mark (liṅga), results in nothing other than inference (anumāna).”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) "And of the meaning that makes [it] understood" means:
one who is timid and righteous should not wander in the region on the banks of the Godāvarī.
In that context, "the state of being a lion" (*siṃhasattva*) refers to the meaning of the indicator (*bodhaka*), by means of the inference "because of the state of being a lion.
"By implication" (*sāmarthyāt*) means "by way of non-deviant concomitance" (*avyabhicārisahacārāt*).
As for the phrase "it results in" (*paryavasyati*), its meaning—that which was stated as "that which results in"—has already been explained previously.
Locanā:

(lo, ū) Regarding the meaning that serves as the indicator (*liṅga*)—namely, the actual presence of the "haughty lion"—it is to be understood through implication (*sāmarthyāt*) as residing in its locus (*āśraya*), which in this context is the bower on the bank of the Godāvarī; thus, there is certainly no absence of [the reason's] presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*) and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛttatva*).

The understanding of the probandum (*sādhya*) would arise from the mark (*liṅga*)—that is, from the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), which is the probandum consisting of the non-wandering that is suggested [by the words].
That is not so; for in this case, regarding the passage beginning with "bhrama abhaimia" (p.

242), it must be said that the wandering enjoined by the cessation of the dog in the house leads to the inference of non-wandering on the banks of the Godāvarī due to the perception of a lion. In that regard, the logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) He restates the opponent's intended point in order to refute it: "That is not so, for...
By "because of the perception of a lion," the meaning is: [a fear] arising from a lion perceived in the words of an unchaste woman.
In the phrase "it causes one to infer," the unfaithful woman is the agent;
in the phrase "it corrupts," the term "anaikāntika" means "deviant."
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) It refutes [the objection], saying "that is not so.
That is not tenable.

To the question "Why is it not logical?", he says: "For thus... Here, "in the house" means this: how indeed could one who, being afraid, has been enjoined to wander in his house once the dog has ceased [to be there], wander at the very place where the dog was perceived? [The reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it deviates from the probandum (*sādhyavyabhicārī*).
Since it is possible for even a timid person to go [to another woman] by the command of a teacher or a master, or out of affection for a beloved,
there is also the fallacy of "doubtful unestablishedness" (*saṃdigdhāsiddhi*) regarding whether the word of a prostitute is authoritative or not.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(Vi, Gha) He demonstrates the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "even of a coward.
"Affection for the beloved" means affection for the beloved who has entered the region of Siṃdhu.
He also shows the fallacy of the reason being doubtful and unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddhi*) with the words "of a wanton woman" (*puṃścalyā*).
The meaning is that because there is doubt regarding the validity of the harlot’s statement,
and because the presence of lions— the reason— on the banks of the Godāvarī is doubtful in one alternative, there is "doubtful unestablishedness" (sāndigdhāsiddhi).
Locanā:
(Lo, ṛ) Why is it inconclusive? To this he says: "even of a coward. After the phrase "by attachment to his beloved," the words "in a place of fear" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The speech of the unchaste woman refers to the words beginning with "O righteous one, wander," and so forth.

Furthermore, it is observed that a hero who fears a dog due to the suspicion of its touch actually goes toward the place where the dog is present out of curiosity for hunting and the like; thus, this is a contradictory inference (*viruddha-hetu*), because the reason adduced proves the opposite of the intended conclusion (*sādhya*), namely, wandering.

Regarding the verse beginning with "jalakeli," one should not say that this is merely an inference (*anumāna*) such as: "He who causes the separation and union of the cakravāka birds through the appearance and disappearance of himself is indeed the moon."
Because [the term] *uttrāsaka* and others are not unambiguous;
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṅa) "water-play."

In such passages as these, he refutes even the notion that the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is inferable, on the grounds that the logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), by means of the example "in the water-play" (*jalakelī*).
[In this case,] the self (*ātman*) possesses a beautiful form;
[the phrase] "in the presence of one who causes alarm, etc. [is used].
For the moon causes terror by bringing about the union and separation of the flock of ruddy geese through its appearance and disappearance;
yet it is not the case that this [moon] is the sun—thus there is a deviation [from the definition].
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sun is included.
Even he, though of such a kind, is not the Moon. Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) "Terrifying"—by whose terrifying clapping of hands and so forth, birds do not alight.
And in the absence of that [intrinsic connection], they come together [only as fallacies]:
even in an inference such as "this very kind of object is the indicator of this very kind of object because it possesses this very kind of nature;
for what is not thus is not so," the reason shares the same status as a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

"Because it has such a nature"—by this very reason, even that which accomplishes such an undesirable [result] is established. In order to refute the demonstration that the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is inferable (*anumeya*) due to the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the establishment of the general [definition], he says "of such a kind" (*evaṃvidha*). *Vijñapriyā*: (vi, ca) He states "of such a kind" in order to also refute the demonstration that the suggested meaning is inferable, because there is no pervasion in the establishment of the general [definition].
The "appearing" (ābhāsamāna) [reason] is the observed deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason, which functions like a crow-scarecrow and consists in its own being seen and not seen.

Because it has such a nature, the reason is "of equal status" (*tattulyayogakṣema*) with that [deviation]; it possesses a deviation equal to that. The meaning is that the reason deviates by being concomitant with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
He demonstrates this with the words: "because it has such a meaning.
Regarding the phrase "of such an undesirable object"—the meaning is that, consequently, the reason (*hetu*) is one that deviates from such an object.
*Locanā*:

The "attainment of security" (*yogakṣema*) is the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) of the manifestation; the sense is that just as the manner of performance consists in the accomplishment of the task, so too does this [manifestation] have such a purpose, for that reason.
He asks, "Why? and says: "In this way."
Likewise, in passages such as "O neighbor, look here for a moment at our house," there is the scraping of the joints of Nala's body.
And her wandering like a stream while alone is said to be the mark of one who possesses the sign (liṅgin) of enjoying the lover of another;
yet, since that [mark] can also occur here through affection for her own husband— as has been stated right here— it is an inconclusive reason.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, cha) In another verse as well, he states—"tathā yaddṛṣṭim"—in order to refute the notion that other suggested meanings are inferable by pointing out the fallacy of the reason; the meaning here is that "strotogamanam" refers to the mention of flowing along a stream.
Herein, the inference is as follows:
"This woman possesses a desire for enjoyment by another lover, because, even though there was the possibility of her breasts being torn by Nala’s knots, she proceeded alone toward the river.
However, although the author has mentioned the striking of the breasts and the proceeding toward the river separately, these do not constitute two separate reasons.
However, those two should be understood as qualifiers of the reason (*hetu*) itself.
He demonstrates the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason with the words "by her own beauty" (*svakāntā*);
by the use of the particle *api*, it should be understood that [the reason deviates] even because of fear of those two.
Locanā: (lo,
ai) By stating "likewise" (*tathā*), she confirms this very intended meaning even through the examples,
demonstrating that the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
