And as for that [inference] of the messenger girl’s enjoyment by her lover in the passage beginning with “The sandalwood paste has completely fallen away” (p. 62), does it occur through the messenger herself as the subject of comprehension,
or through others who were present at that time?
Or [the suggestion may be grasped] by sensitive readers through the contemplation of the meaning of that poem.

*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ja): In order to refute the view that even in verses such as "niḥśeṣacyuta... the suggested fact of the female messenger’s enjoyment by her lover is merely inferable, he says: "And that which... (yacceti).
There is no dispute regarding the first two [cases];
however, in the third case, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in instances where such an intention is absent.
Vijñapriyā:
(Vi, Jha) "There is no dispute regarding the first two cases"—meaning that, first of all, an inference performed by the female messenger is simply not possible;
for since her utility [in that regard] is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Furthermore, if the people present at that time were not perceivers of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), then there could be no inference for them either; thus, there is likewise no dispute in that case as well.
If, however, [the object] is the cognizer of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyaboddhṛ*), then its inclusion occurs precisely within the third position; this is the meaning.

Since that which is the object of the spectator’s cognition—and which alone is to be relished—is what I am investigating, it is only there that [the suggested meaning] is inferable, given the dispute over its inferability.
He refutes its inferability with the words: "But in the third [position]," etc.
The meaning is as follows: the intention of the messenger (dūtī) is the intention to enjoy her lover;

since the falling off of sandalwood paste and so forth does not possess the property of being pervaded by enjoyment in the absence of that [lover], there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that very case. — *Locanā*

(Lo, o) "There is no dispute" means: indeed, we do not deny the inference [of the messenger's presence] from her or from those situated near her at that time. "Of such a kind" means: indeed, [it is not as if one were inferring] from the phrase, "The sandalwood paste has completely vanished."
The meaning is that the intention of such an explanatory passage has been made an object of certainty by someone.
Now, one might object: "It should not be said that the reason is qualified by being accompanied by the states of the speaker and so forth. [To this, the author replies:
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ña) He says "the state of the speaker and so forth" (*vaktrādyavasthā*) in order to refute the claim that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by providing qualifiers such as "having desisted from bathing and the like.
The meaning is "the state of the speaker and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the drawing of the breasts, kissing, and scratching with the nails are included.
The state (*avasthā*), however, is the condition of intense passion (*rati*).
Thus, the meaning is that the cause of the falling of sandalwood paste and so forth should be qualified by its being accompanied by such a state and other factors.
*Locanā*.

"Lo, au" (*nanu*): the meaning is that the state which the speaker reached before speaking in such a manner must be used as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*), because there is an absence of any such consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*). — *Vijñapriyā*.
(vi, ṭa) He provides the explanation: "of such a kind" (*evaṃvidha*).
This means [the consideration of pervasion] as constituted by such qualifying attributes;
for indeed, such qualifying attributes do not exist in the verse.
By the word "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) and so forth, there is the inclusion of such a qualified reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, since such poetic compositions, being born solely from the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*), do not necessarily possess validity, the reason is "unestablished due to doubt" (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭha) Therein, he also demonstrates the fallacious nature of the reason with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*).

By the phrase "due to the non-necessity of [the speaker's] authority" (*prāmāṇyānāvaśyakatvena*), the meaning is as follows: even if the speaker does not mention the falling away of sandalwood paste and so forth, it is entirely possible for the poet to recount those statements;
therefore, the audience must infer the erotic enjoyment (*sambhoga*) based on the falling away of sandalwood paste and so forth obtained from the words recounted by the poet.
The meaning is that it is "doubtful" because of the uncertainty as to whether that sandalwood and so forth is explicitly mentioned or not mentioned by the speaker.
Locanā:
(lo, a) "Furthermore"—this refers to the fallacy of being "unestablished due to doubt" (sandigdhāsiddha); for a poet does not describe only an object that is already established [as a fact].
Furthermore, the proponent of suggestion (vyañjanāvādin) has stated that these word-meanings possess suggestiveness only when accompanied by the term *adhamā* (lowly woman);
therefore, how can there be an inference as to whether the lover's lowliness is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) or not?
*Vijñapriyā*:

(Vi, ḍa) Now, one might object: "How can there be even a suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of enjoyment according to your view, by means of such [causes] as the falling of sandalwood paste, which are either transitory (*vyabhicārin*) or doubtful? To this he says: "And by the proponent of *vyakti*.
This means "by the proponent of *vyañjanā*.
The meaning is that it was stated thus because the status of being a suggestor (*vyañjakatva*) is established through the force of the result (*phala*).

The point is that, unlike in the case of inference (*anumāna*), deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth do not constitute a constituent factor even in the case of suggestion (*vyañjanā*). He states—by the words "and by that"—that even the provision of a qualification such as "being sent by one who is base" is not possible in the case of inference; the meaning is that "by that" refers to the baseness expressed by the word *adhama*.
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood that even if inferiority (*adhamatva*) were established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), inference would still be impossible on that basis alone, provided there exists a desire to go to a female messenger (*dūtīgamana-icchā-rāditva*).
— *Locanā* —

By this, the proponent of manifestation (*vyañjanāvādin*), who has exerted himself to establish the function of manifestation (*vyañjanāvyāpāra*), has refuted the view that manifested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) are to be known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
This is because it is established [in the scriptures] that "one should not stand near a low person" (*adhamapadaṃ na punastasyādhamasyāntikam iti*).
By this, even the claim that manifested meanings are cognizable through presumptive testimony is cast aside.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) also proceeds only by depending upon a previously established pervasion (*vyāpti*) and a desire [to know].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍha): By this [statement], "presumption," he also refutes the view that suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) are cognizable through presumption.
"Vyāpticchāyām" means the shadow of pervasion, that is to say, the manner of pervasion characterized by invariable concomitance.
Locanā:
By "etena"—that is, by this demonstration of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) in inference.
Why? He says: "Even from presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
This refers to the shadow of a pervasion previously apprehended, such as:
"Whoever lives, stays somewhere."
"He lives here in the assembly, yet Caitra is not present," and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṇa): He shows such a concomitance [of existence and non-existence] in the words "he who lives."
He demonstrates the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that proceeds by depending upon that [inference] with the words "if he lives" (*jīvati cet*).
Therefore, the meaning obtained through *arthāpatti* is that "this exists in a place other than the cow-pen.

Thus, the point is that in the examples shown, there can be no *arthāpatti*, because it is impossible for it to depend on the shadow of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) when the reason (*hetu*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Locanā:
(lo, ī) If, indeed, one were to ascertain the location [of something] while it was previously alive;
for the nature of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is that what has been seen or heard cannot otherwise be accounted for.
The postulation of that [unperceived] object for the sake of that [perceived fact] is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Regarding this, the Bhaṭṭas explain: "the perceived" (*dṛṣṭa*) means apprehended by the five means of valid cognition characterized as perception, inference, analogy, presumptive testimony, and non-existence. And he specifies it separately from the "heard" (*śruta*) in order to demonstrate the primacy of verbal testimony.
"Known through hearing" means that a specific object known by way of the definition of a word cannot be otherwise accounted for.
This is because it is observed that a verbal expectancy is fulfilled only by a word—as in the case of:
"Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day."
In this context, the phrase "he eats at night" is supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
However, the teacher Prabhākara says: "Seen or heard"—this is a worldly expression used out of disregard [for the literal].
Therefore, it functions merely as a perception established by worldly convention,
and not for the purpose of establishing conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For since a word is postulated as a means to cognize an object when other means are remote, it would be better to postulate that [cognition] directly upon the object itself.
Therefore, in Bhaṭṭa’s view, regarding presumptive testimony based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*),
the statement "he eats at night" is postulated.
In the Guru’s view, however, in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the eating at night is indeed the object [of the presumption].
Thus, let not a specific sentence be postulated here;
rather, in the Guru’s view, in the case of presumptive testimony, the eating at night is the very object itself.
Thus, let not a specific sentence be postulated here; do not think so.

In cases such as "Devadatta is fat," [the inference] regarding his eating at night, or "Caitra, though alive, is not present here in this assembly," [the inference] regarding his being somewhere else proceeds by depending solely upon an apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) previously experienced. Therefore, it is *arthāpatti* (presumption).
The sense is that since suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) are not objects of inference (*anumāna*), they cannot be objects of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
"Pervasion" (*vyāpti*) is the rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*).
He shows the nature of pervasion with the words "as follows" (*yathā*).

Furthermore, this [number] is not something cognizable by a suggestive cognition— such as the cognition of the number ten through the lifting of the index finger during the sale of cloth and similar instances—
because even a suggestive cognition is admitted to be a form of inference since it depends upon worldly means of knowledge such as convention (*saṅketa*).
(Vijñapriyā)

(vi, ta) Regarding the view held by some that "indication" (*sūcanā*) is a certain operation and that the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is understood through it alone—the author states "furthermore" (*kiñca*) in order to refute that position.

The phrase "like the number ten and so forth" means that just as the number ten and so on are understood through the cognition of indication dependent upon the balancing of the index finger and other fingers, so too is the suggested meaning.
He establishes his own doctrine—that indication is included within inference—by stating: "of the cognition of indication as well."
The nature of inference is the very essence of inferential cognition.
Thus, if there is no suspicion of deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the weighing of a finger and so forth, there is inference in that case.

However, in the case of the falling of sandalwood paste and the like, because deviation is perceived, the cognition of sexual enjoyment and so forth is dependent solely upon the manifestation of indicative signs (vyañjana); this is the intended meaning.
Locanā:

(Lo, u) Now, since suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) are not the objects of inference, they are also not the objects of the means of knowledge known as "presumption" (*ceṣṭā*); thus he says—"Furthermore" (*kiñca*). This refers to the suggested meaning.

By the phrase "due to dependence on worldly means of valid cognition such as conventions," he refers to the restatement of the grasped pervasion (*vyāpti*), namely: "Wherever there is the pointing upward of the index finger, there is the number ten.

Furthermore, regarding the claim by some that "the cognition of taste and so forth is memory because it is produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)," even in that case, the reason is fallacious due to its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) with respect to recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, tha) In order to refute the view of those who maintain that the cognition of taste and so forth is of the nature of memory because it is produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), he says: "In that case also... And this [refutation] is merely superficial.
In every respect, the reason "being produced by mental impressions" (*saṃskārajanyatva*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).
However, the fault lies rather in the impossibility of [rasa] being a memory, given that its nature is self-luminous bliss (*svaprakāśānanda*). — *Locanā*.

(Lo, Ū) He clarifies the meaning of the verse-quarter "smṛtir na ca rasādidhīḥ" with the words "yañca": "And moreover... [He states that] there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) because even recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which takes the form of knowledge such as "This is that Devadatta," is produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), as seen in the passage beginning with "durgālaṅghita-" (on page 59).
Furthermore, as for what Mahimabhaṭṭa stated—that there is no such thing as a second object—that is merely the "closing of eyes like an elephant" of one who denies what is established by experience.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, da):
The phrase "there is no such thing as a second object in the form of Maheśvara" means that it does not exist as an object of cognition; this refers to the word "denying."
"Upari" (above/above this), such is the ellipsis.
"Gajanimīlikā" refers to contemptuous indifference.
Locanā:
"Like the closing of eyes by an elephant"—this means that even without critical reflection, one speaks while closing both eyes like an intoxicated elephant out of fear of public censure.

Thus, it is established that a fourth function (*vṛtti*) must indeed be cultivated; for the meaning characterized by the various *rasas* and so forth is proven by experience and cannot be denied; it follows the positive and negative concomitance of those respective words and so forth;

it is not accessible through means of knowledge such as inference; and it is not cognizable by the three functions beginning with denotation (*abhidhā*). Therefore, this fourth function is to be honored.
Locanā:
This has been explained in detail right here in the second chapter.
He concludes: "Thus, in this way... [tadevam].
And since this [aesthetic relish] occurs even without the mental synthesis of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, it is entirely stainless.
Locanā:

(lo, ḷ) Nor should it be argued that because it is the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and other factors as presented by words alone that generates the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, poetry does not function here as a direct cause.

According to the maxim that "one's own limb does not obstruct," because the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) belongs to the poem itself through the intermediate operation of making manifest the excitants (*vibhāva*), the Bhaṭṭas, Naiyāyikas, and others accept that the words themselves are the instrument (*karaṇa*), just as they [accept] that for those who bring about the connection with an object by means of the cognition of their own referents, it is the words alone that are the instrument.

Furthermore, according to the principle that "an operation must have a door [of access]," the causality of the cognition of the combination of the *vibhāvas* and other factors toward aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) is impossible, because there is no intervening operation in between.

Now, one might object: "In that case, if the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) were understood suddenly without the consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, how would there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And this...

[referring to the verse]. Even without production [of a new cognition], the comprehension of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), which is established by experience, occurs precisely through the logical necessity of another meaning.
What, then, is this function called?
It is said: "This function of the phonemes (vyañjanas) is called *vṛtti* by the wise;
however, others know the function pertaining to the manifestation of rasa as being called *rasanā*. (VisSd 5.5)
And this has been explained in detail in the section on the definition of *rasa*; thus everything is clear.
Regarding the statement that some call the manifestation of *rasa* "tasting" (*rasana*), he says: "But as for the manifestation of *rasa*... (*rasavyaktau punar iti*).
"In the function of rasa" (rasavṛttau) means "in the function that makes rasa known.
In this way, the mere fact that the cognition of the suggested meaning is of the nature of mental perception (mānasabuddhi) has not been refuted.
The intention here is as follows: the mind, for its part, possesses no independence whatsoever with respect to external objects.
However, the theory that there is a "manifestation" (*bodhana*) of the suggested meaning through the assistance of the application of memory is refuted by the very impossibility of such recollection,

since the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consisting of the aforementioned bliss, or the object consisting of the lover’s union and so forth [as represented by] the female messenger, has never been experienced before.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Maheśvara Nyāyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya.
Locanā:
(Lo, e) The intention is that the conceptualization of the operation of *vyañjanā* belongs to the venerable teacher Ānandavardhana.
He recalls the fact that rasa is manifested through the operation of tasting (*rasana*) by stating "rasanā" [etc.].
In the context of the exposition on *rasa*,

within the commentary on the verse beginning with "due to the predominance of *sattva*," the term "all" refers to the entire range of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) that establish the function of *vyañjanā*.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Establishment of the Function of Suggestion," in the *Locana* commentary on the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*;
thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, titled "The Exposition of the Function of Suggestion."
